digest.top_line: Dose-adapted single-isocenter SRS for 4-10 BM: 22 of 40 pts outlived DS-GPA prediction (bar was 17), 1-yr local failure 5%, no G3-5 AEs.
digest.tldr: All-CNS day on SRS technique for brain mets. The prospective dose-adapted SIMT trial (4-10 BM) cleared its DS-GPA survival bar with 1-yr local failure 5%; retrospective Minniti and HyperArc series report 1-yr LC 89% and 90.1%. The planning comparisons trade V12Gy against low-dose spill and report dosimetric surrogates only.

sites.intro: Five SRS technique studies for BM; only the dose-adapted SIMT trial is prospective, and the planning comparisons carry no clinical endpoints.

studies.name: DCAT vs CoVMAT vs NcVMAT for single brain metastasis (planning study)
studies.tldr: Non-coplanar VMAT gave the lowest normal-brain V12Gy (9.4 vs 11.6 DCAT vs 15.1 cm3 coplanar VMAT) for 2-3 cm single BM SRS plans.
details: 🔍 Planning study, 15 pts with single BM, longest diameter 2-3 cm, single institution (Kyoto)
🔍 Each pt re-planned 3 ways: DCAT, coplanar VMAT (1 arc), non-coplanar VMAT (1 coplanar + 2 couch arcs)

subdetails: 20 Gy x 1 to PTV, normalized to D99.5%
PTV = GTV + 1mm; median PTV 6.4 cm3 (range 3.7-16.2)
6 MV TrueBeam STx; Eclipse 15.6, AcurosXB, 1mm grid
VMAT plans used a ring contour + Normal Tissue Objective

details: 📊 RTOG-CI and Paddick CI better with NcVMAT vs DCAT; GTV D98% higher with NcVMAT vs both
⚠️ Coplanar-only VMAT was worse than DCAT on V15Gy through V5Gy; low-dose spill was the largest at V5Gy
📐 Beam-on time longer for both VMAT techniques vs DCAT; MUs lower with CoVMAT
⚠️ Dosimetric surrogate only: no local control, radionecrosis, or neurocognitive outcome measured
🔗 Molinier et al. compared the same 3 techniques across mixed intracranial lesions but with different TPS/algorithms; here one TPS used throughout

verdict.rationale: Single-institution planning study, N=15; V12Gy and conformity are dosimetric surrogates, with no clinical radionecrosis or local control endpoint.
verdict.audience: Single brain metastasis, 2-3 cm, LINAC single-fraction SRS

studies.significance: Coplanar-only VMAT, the default at many LINAC centers, was the worst of the three for normal brain, with V12Gy 15.1 vs 11.6 cm3 for DCAT and V5Gy 96.8 vs 49.2 cm3. The gain from VMAT comes from the couch arcs, not modulation alone, which bears on technique choice for 2-3 cm lesions where V12Gy drives radionecrosis risk.
studies.monday_clinic: For a 2-3 cm single brain metastasis planned for single-fraction LINAC SRS, this supports non-coplanar VMAT over a coplanar-only arc on normal-brain V12Gy; it does not address multiple metastases, fractionated SRS, or clinical radionecrosis rates.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **planning study**: each of **15 pts** re-planned with DCAT, CoVMAT, and NcVMAT in the same TPS. Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc for target indices; repeated-measures ANOVA with Holm post-hoc for normal-brain doses.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pts treated April 2016 to October 2017 for a **single brain metastasis, longest diameter 2-3 cm**. Median PTV 6.4 cm3 (range 3.7-16.2).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **20 Gy in 1 fraction** to PTV (GTV + 1mm), normalized to D99.5%, PTV D2% set near 142% of prescription. 6 MV TrueBeam STx; DCAT and NcVMAT shared one coplanar arc plus couch arcs at 60 and 300 degrees.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: RTOG-CI, Paddick CI, PTV and GTV dose indices, normal-brain V20Gy to V5Gy, MUs, and beam-on time. No clinical endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: NcVMAT gave **lower V20Gy, V15Gy, V12Gy, V10Gy and V5Gy** than both comparators, plus better CIs and GTV D98% than DCAT. Beam-on time was longer for both VMAT plans than for DCAT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Molinier et al. is the only prior direct three-way comparison, but it pooled primary brain tumors and single and multiple mets, with different TPS, algorithms, and prescriptions. Vogelbaum et al. is cited for higher local recurrence and radionecrosis above 2.0 cm, which is why this lesion size was chosen.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents single 2-3 cm brain metastases planned for single-fraction LINAC SRS with a 1mm PTV margin. Does not represent multiple metastases, single-isocenter multi-target plans, fractionated SRS, or Gamma Knife.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Plans optimized by the investigators in one TPS, so planner skill and the ring-contour approach may not transfer. Large SDs on low-dose volumes, and longer beam-on with non-coplanar arcs raises intrafraction motion questions that were not measured.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for non-coplanar VMAT rests on **V12Gy as a radionecrosis surrogate** and on lowering low and intermediate dose for long survivors who may need repeat SRS. Whether these volume differences change clinical radionecrosis rates is not tested.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful finding here is not that non-coplanar VMAT won, but that coplanar-only VMAT lost to the older technique. Many centers moved from DCAT to VMAT and kept the delivery coplanar for speed and simpler couch workflow. In this dataset that trade gave up normal-brain sparing compared with DCAT at every level from V15Gy down to V5Gy, and the low-dose bath (V5Gy 96.8 vs 49.2 cm3) was the largest gap. Inverse optimization alone did not make up for losing the couch arcs. When the couch arcs went back in, VMAT pulled ahead of DCAT on every normal-brain metric and on conformity. So the geometry of the arcs explains most of the effect, and modulation adds a smaller increment on top.

The clinical argument depends entirely on V12Gy as a stand-in for radionecrosis risk, which the authors present as an accepted predictor while noting that thresholds vary by modality, lesion type, and size. Lesions of 2-3 cm are where that surrogate matters most, since this is the size band in which Vogelbaum and colleagues reported higher local recurrence and radionecrosis than for smaller lesions. The NcVMAT advantage (V12Gy 9.4 vs 11.6 cm3 for DCAT) is real on paper, but the SDs are wide and no outcome was measured. Whether a difference of this size moves the risk of symptomatic necrosis is the open question, and a planning study cannot answer it.

Several design choices should temper confidence. The plans were made by the study team in one TPS with one algorithm. That removes the cross-system confounding that weakened Molinier's earlier comparison, but it means the result reflects this group's planning practice, including a ring contour and Normal Tissue Objective that a different planner might use differently. Prescription and normalization were matched, yet DCAT was shaped by hand-edited MLCs to hit a D2% target, so DCAT quality is also operator-dependent. With 15 pts, single lesions, and a 1mm margin, the result does not cover multi-target single-isocenter plans, larger margins, or fractionated SRS, which many centers now use at 2-3 cm.

The cost side is beam-on time: both VMAT plans took longer than DCAT, and non-coplanar arcs add couch moves. On a frameless mask workflow, longer delivery means more chance of intrafraction motion, and a 1mm margin leaves little room for it. That cost was not measured here.

For practice, the defensible read is narrow. If a center plans VMAT for a solitary 2-3 cm metastasis, the data argue against dropping the non-coplanar arcs, and they give no support for coplanar VMAT over DCAT. Showing NcVMAT is clinically better would take outcome data on radionecrosis and local control, ideally across several planners and systems.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Coplanar-only VMAT gave more normal-brain dose than DCAT (V12Gy 15.1 vs 11.6 cm3), and adding couch arcs reversed it (9.4 cm3). For 2-3 cm single-lesion SRS, the non-coplanar geometry, not modulation alone, drives the V12Gy gain.

open_questions: Does lower V12Gy with NcVMAT reduce clinical radionecrosis?
Does the advantage hold for multiple metastases or fractionated SRS?
Does longer beam-on time add intrafraction motion error?

studies.name: Elements MME vs RapidArc single-isocenter SRS plan quality
studies.tldr: RapidArc VMAT gave lower V12Gy (19.2 vs 23.7 cm3) and better conformity; Elements MME gave lower V5Gy and mean brain dose (2.57 vs 2.76 Gy).
details: 🔍 Two-institution treatment planning study: 30 pts, each replanned with both techniques (60 plans)
🔍 4 to 10 brain mets per pt (217 targets, median 7.5); total PTV median 7.05 cm3
🔍 Each center planned its own technique: TJU Elements MME v1.5, UAB Eclipse RapidArc 13.6

subdetails: Rx 14 to 24 Gy single fraction, normalized to D99% = Rx
MME: 4 to 9 noncoplanar DCAs, 6 MV FFF, pencil-beam calc
RA: 2 to 4 noncoplanar VMAT arcs, 10 MV FFF, AAA calc
Both HD120 MLC, 1 mm dose grid, DVH analysis in third-party MIM

details: 📊 RA lower V12Gy in 26 of 30 cases; MME lower V5Gy in 25 of 30
📊 Exceptions to the V12Gy pattern were all small total PTV (<2.1 cm3); there MME won V12Gy in 4 of 6
📊 Brain DVHs cross near 6 Gy: RA favorable above, MME favorable below
📊 Mean coverage 97.5% MME vs 96.9% RA (P=.007)
💊 Delivery: MME 7.3 arcs, 6871 MU, est. beam-on 6 to 9 min; RA 3.8 arcs, 10225 MU, est. 3 to 4 min
🔗 vs Gevaert (10 pts, 40 mets): Paddick CI 0.65/0.67 there vs 0.70/0.77 here, suggesting under-optimized plans in that series
🔗 vs Narayanasamy (8 pts, 40 targets): found the techniques comparable, likely underpowered
⚠️ Beam energy (6 vs 10 MV FFF) and planning institution are confounded with technique
⚠️ Dosimetric surrogates only; no radionecrosis, control or cognitive outcomes
⚠️ Abstract and Results disagree on RA median RTOG CI (1.21 vs 1.23)
⚠️ Several authors hold Varian research support or consulting ties

verdict.rationale: Dosimetric surrogates only, no clinical endpoints; beam energy and planning institution confounded with technique; software versions predate HyperArc.
verdict.audience: 4 to 10 brain mets, single-isocenter linac SRS, 14 to 24 Gy x1

studies.significance: The V12Gy advantage for RapidArc depends on total target volume: every case where MME matched or beat it had total PTV under 2.1 cm3, and above that threshold the V12 ratio averaged 1.24. V12Gy is the metric tied to radionecrosis, so for multi-met SRS the planning platform matters most in larger-volume cases.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts with 4 to 10 brain mets and total PTV above 2.1 cm3 planned for single-isocenter linac SRS, this supports VMAT when V12Gy is the binding constraint; it does not apply to HyperArc, >10 targets, or centers without expert VMAT planning.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Two-institution **treatment planning comparison**: 15 previously treated pts from each center were replanned at the other center with the other technique, giving **30 pts, 60 plans**. Metrics extracted in third-party software (MIM) to remove TPS-dependent DVH differences.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **4 to 10 brain metastases** per pt, 217 targets, median 7.5. Individual target volume 0.014 to 17.73 cm3; total PTV 0.49 to 27.32 cm3, median 7.05 cm3.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **14 to 24 Gy single fraction**, prescriptions unchanged between plans, normalized so 99% of target volume received Rx. MME: 4 to 9 noncoplanar DCAs, **6 MV FFF**. RA: one 360 axial arc plus up to three noncoplanar half arcs, **10 MV FFF**, UAB three-ring tuning-structure method.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: RTOG and Paddick CI per target; V12Gy, V8Gy, V5Gy and mean brain dose per plan; arcs, MU and estimated beam-on time. Paired 2-tailed Wilcoxon at .05.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Both platforms met clinical goals in all cases. **RA favored above roughly 6 Gy** (conformity, V12Gy, V8Gy), **MME favored below** (V5Gy, mean brain dose), with the MME low-dose edge largest at small total PTV.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Larger than prior head-to-head series: Gevaert (10 pts, 40 mets) and Narayanasamy (8 pts, 40 targets). Gevaert's Paddick CI of 0.65 and 0.67 vs **0.70 and 0.77** here suggests earlier comparisons understated both platforms, MME partly from the v1.0 to v1.5 optimizer change.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents 4 to 10 brain mets planned with single-isocenter linac SRS by experienced planners on MME v1.5 or Eclipse 13.6. Does not represent HyperArc, later MME versions, >10 targets, fractionated SRS, or less experienced VMAT planners.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Treatment time could not be measured directly in a replanning study. Hotspot and maximum target dose were not compared. RA plan quality reflects one expert planner, and the authors note VMAT quality depends on the planner.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trade is **moderate-dose spill vs low-dose spill**. V8 to V12Gy has retrospective links to radionecrosis, while low-dose spill has none yet, though the authors argue cumulative low dose may matter for cognition after repeat SRS or later WBRT.

studies.interpretation:
The practical question here is narrower than the abstract suggests. Both platforms produced clinically acceptable plans in all 30 cases, so the study is not choosing between an adequate and an inadequate tool. It is describing a dose-level trade. RapidArc wins wherever dose is moderate to high (conformity, V12Gy, V8Gy) and Elements MME wins below roughly 6 Gy (V5Gy, mean brain dose). Which side of that trade matters depends on which toxicity a reader believes in. V8Gy to V12Gy has retrospective associations with radionecrosis, while low-dose spill has no established toxicity correlate. On current evidence the RapidArc advantage sits on the better-validated metric, and the MME advantage rests on a cognitive hypothesis the authors raise but do not test.

The size of the differences matters as much as their direction. V5Gy medians of 141.4 and 142.8 cm3 are almost identical. The P value of .009 comes from consistent per-case pairing (MME lower in 25 of 30), not from a meaningful gap in typical volume. Mean brain dose of 2.57 vs 2.76 Gy is the same story. The V12Gy gap of 23.7 vs 19.2 cm3, holding in 26 of 30 cases, is the difference most likely to carry clinical weight. The volume dependence is the most useful finding for planning: every case where MME matched or beat RapidArc on V12Gy had total PTV under 2.1 cm3, and above that threshold the V12 ratio averaged 1.24. A reader with a small-volume, many-target case loses little with MME. A reader with larger total volume has a dosimetric reason to prefer VMAT.

Three design features should limit how far this transfers. First, technique is confounded with beam energy (6 vs 10 MV FFF), dose algorithm (pencil beam vs AAA) and institution. The authors suspect the energy difference affects penumbra and low-dose volume most for small targets, which is exactly where MME looked best. Part of the small-PTV MME advantage may therefore be a beam effect rather than a technique effect. Second, RapidArc quality is planner-dependent, and every VMAT plan came from one expert using a refined in-house method with more than 1000 cases behind it. MME, being template-driven, is easier to reproduce. A center without that VMAT experience should expect its own RapidArc plans to fall short of these, which narrows or reverses the V12Gy edge. The authors' own contrast with Gevaert's Paddick CI of 0.67 for RA makes this point. Third, the software is dated: MME v1.5 and Eclipse 13.6 without automated collimator selection for island blocking. HyperArc is named as the next comparison, so today's VMAT versus today's MME is not answered here.

Delivery efficiency also cuts in RapidArc's favor despite higher MU (10225 vs 6871), because it uses fewer arcs and couch positions, with estimated beam-on of 3 to 4 vs 6 to 9 minutes. These are estimates from a replanning study, not measured treatment times. Vendor ties appear on one side of the comparison, which makes the authors' willingness to report MME advantages somewhat reassuring, but they still warrant noting.

What would make this wrong is a link between low-dose brain spill and cognition in long survivors receiving serial radiosurgery. If such a link were shown, the MME advantage would gain weight. Until then, the result supports platform choice by total target volume and planner expertise rather than a single winner.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: RapidArc's V12Gy advantage holds above 2.1 cm3 total PTV (V12 ratio mean 1.24) and disappears below it, where MME won V12Gy in 4 of 6 cases. Because V12Gy tracks radionecrosis risk, total target volume and VMAT planner expertise should guide the platform choice for multi-met SRS.

open_questions: Does lower V12Gy with VMAT translate into less radionecrosis?
Does cumulative low-dose brain spill affect cognition after repeat SRS?
How do HyperArc and newer MME versions compare?

studies.tldr: 1-yr LC 89%, 1-yr OS 68%, no G3-4 toxicity after single-isocenter DCA SRS for 4-10 BM; a 1-mm GTV-to-PTV margin kept dose coverage on every lesion.

🔍 Median clinical f/u 11 mo (range 4-26); 13 (42%) pts alive at data cutoff

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective series of **31 consecutive pts** with **204 BM** at two Italian centers, Oct 2016 to Sep 2018. Median clinical f/u **11 mo** (range 4-26).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with **4 to 10 BM <3 cm**. Median age 60; histologies lung 14, melanoma 8, breast 5, kidney 3, ovary 1. Median total GTV 3.8 cm3 (range 1.4-9.9).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-isocenter DCA SRS planned with Brainlab Elements Multiple Brain Mets SRS v1.5, **20-22 Gy** for lesions <2 cm and **16-18 Gy** for ≥2 cm or near critical structures. PTV = GTV + **1 mm** (n=176) or 2 mm (n=28), with ExacTrac 6D setup and intrafraction correction at 0.5 mm / 0.5° tolerance.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Local control, OS and distant brain failure by KM from SRS; toxicity by CTCAE v5. Dosimetric endpoints were V95 and D95 after CBCT-based reconstruction of residual isocenter error.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Coverage loss (V95 <95%) hit **28 targets** and tracked with distance from isocenter (P=.0001) and small volume (P=.015). A **1-mm margin restored coverage for all lesions**; with 0 mm, 18 lesions remained compromised.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No G3-4 toxicity.** Radionecrosis in 5 (16.1%) pts, G2 motor deficit in 2; per-lesion risk 11% at 12 mo, driven by **V12Gy >10 cm3** (P=.01).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors place the 89% 1-yr LC alongside published single-target and single-isocenter SRS series for up to 10 BM. Plan quality (CI 1.32, GI 3.94) is described as in line with DCA and VMAT reports, including Ruggeri's Brainlab vs HyperArc comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with 4-10 BM <3 cm and cumulative tumor volume <15 cm3, treated frameless with 6D intrafraction monitoring. Does not represent >10 BM, lesions ≥3 cm, or delivery without intrafraction imaging and correction.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The paper is internally inconsistent on lesion-count strata and on how many pts had coverage loss. Margin adequacy was judged dosimetrically on offline CBCT fusion, not against lesion-level local failure, and no neurocognitive testing was done.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support a 1-mm margin as a middle ground between coverage and the V12Gy growth that larger margins bring. Whether that holds without 6D correction, or how hippocampal and normal-brain dose affect cognition, is left open.

studies.interpretation:
The question this series addresses is narrower than its title suggests. Single-isocenter multi-target SRS already has a dosimetric literature showing plan quality comparable to one isocenter per lesion. What has been missing is evidence that small rotational errors at a shared isocenter do not quietly underdose the lesions farthest from it. Roper's VMAT simulation, cited by the authors, found little coverage loss at 0.5° but meaningful loss at 2°, and that has pushed some groups toward larger margins. Minniti's group measured the residual error their system actually achieves, reconstructed its dosimetric consequence lesion by lesion, and asked what margin absorbs it. That is the useful contribution, and it should be read as a technique-validation study with clinical outcomes attached, not as an outcomes study.

The central finding cuts in two directions. Under ExacTrac 6D correction the mean 3D residual error was 0.34 mm, and a 1-mm margin preserved coverage for every lesion, while a 0-mm simulation left 18 lesions underdosed. So zero-margin single-isocenter delivery is not supported here, even with good imaging. But the intrafraction analysis is the real caveat: when out-of-tolerance shifts were left uncorrected, GTV coverage fell in 21 of 74 lesions. The 1-mm margin is therefore a property of the whole workflow, not of the planning software. A center without repeated intrafraction imaging should not borrow it.

The pattern of failure in coverage matches the geometry. Loss concentrated in small lesions far from isocenter, under 0.40 cm3 and at or beyond 39 mm. This is the subgroup where margin choice and isocenter placement both matter, and where a planner might reasonably add margin selectively rather than uniformly. Table 4 makes the cost concrete: a 1-mm expansion on a 1-cm sphere takes the volume from 0.52 to 0.9 cm3. Given that V12Gy above 10 cm3 predicted radionecrosis here (P=.01), and that the Korytko gamma knife data quoted by the authors put radionecrosis at 55.3% above that threshold, the case for keeping the margin minimal is dosimetric and clinical at once.

The clinical outcomes are reassuring but cannot carry much weight. With 31 pts, a median follow-up of 11 mo and 13 pts alive at cutoff, the 2-yr estimates rest on few patients at risk. Local control was assessed against a historical benchmark, not a concurrent multi-isocenter cohort. The dosimetric endpoint, V95 on offline CBCT fusion, was never linked to which lesions actually failed, so the paper cannot show that the underdosed lesions recurred more often. The radionecrosis rate of 16.1% of pts is not trivial for a cohort whose cumulative volumes were modest, and KPS is a coarse substitute for neurocognitive testing in a technique whose main selling point over WBRT is cognitive preservation.

The abstract and results also disagree on the lesion-count strata and on how many patients had coverage loss. That does not change the margin conclusion, but it lowers confidence in the reporting overall. What would make the 1-mm recommendation wrong is a lesion-level local-failure analysis showing excess recurrence in small distal targets, or a cohort treated without 6D correction. Neither is tested here.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Uncorrected intrafraction shifts dropped GTV coverage in 21 (28%) of 74 lesions, so the 1-mm margin only holds alongside 6D intrafraction correction. Coverage loss clustered in lesions <0.40 cm3 and ≥39 mm from isocenter, the targets where margin and isocenter placement decide the plan.

open_questions: Neurocognitive outcome with formal testing after single-isocenter SRS
Does the 1-mm margin hold without 6D intrafraction correction?

studies.name: Dose-adapted single-isocenter multitarget SRS for 4-10 brain mets
studies.tldr: mOS 8.1 mo, 1-yr OS 35.7%; 22 of 40 pts outlived DS-GPA prediction (bar was 17), 1-yr local failure 5%, no G3-5 AEs.
details: 📊 mOS 8.1 mo, 6-mo OS 57.3%, 1-yr OS 35.7% from protocol SRS
📐 DS-GPA predicted mOS 5.5 mo, 1-yr 20% for this cohort
📐 22 of 40 pts outlived DS-GPA prediction; prespecified noninferiority bar was 17
🔍 Prospective single-arm, N=40, Durham NC, accrued Feb 2017 to Aug 2019, median f/u 15.2 mo

rows: 20 Gy (<2 cm) or 18 Gy (2 to <3 cm)

details: 📊 1-yr local failure 5% (2.6%, 8.7%): 10 of 204 lesions, in 4 of 32 pts
📊 Distant brain failure cumulative incidence 20% at 6 mo, 35.8% at 12 mo

subdetails: G1-2 SIMT-related AEs in 73%, no G3-5
Headache 50%, fatigue 45%, nausea 25%, alopecia 20%
Radionecrosis in 5 lesions (4 pts), 1-yr rate 1.5%
Neurologic death 20%
MMSE, Trail Making, HVLT, FACT-Br unchanged at 3 mo

details: 🔍 Median beam-on 8 min; median table time 31.5 min/d
⚠️ Benchmark is DS-GPA predicted survival, not a randomized WBRT or multi-isocenter arm
⚠️ 11 pts had prior SRS/WBRT, while DS-GPA times survival from first brain met diagnosis
⚠️ Discussion cites 58% 6-mo distant brain failure; Results report 20%
⚠️ Funded by Varian Medical Systems

verdict.rationale: Prospective but single-arm, N=40, benchmarked against DS-GPA predicted survival rather than a randomized WBRT or multi-isocenter comparator; vendor-funded.
verdict.audience: 4-10 brain mets, non-SCLC histologies, KPS ≥70, largest lesion ≤4 cm

studies.significance: The transferable piece is the switch rule: if single-fraction brain V12Gy exceeded 20 mL or any lesion was in the brainstem, every lesion got 25 Gy/5 fx. Those 79 lesions had 98% LC and 1.3% radionecrosis, vs 93% and 3.4% with single fraction (P=NS). Aggregate volume, not lesion count, decides whether to fractionate.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts with 4-10 brain mets, KPS ≥70 and lesions ≤4 cm, this gives prospective support for SRS alone in place of WBRT; it does not extend to SCLC, leptomeningeal disease, more than 10 mets, or pts who cannot get MRI every 3 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **single-arm** trial, N=40, Feb 2017 to Aug 2019, NCT02886572. Noninferiority was defined as **≥17 of 40 pts** outliving their original DS-GPA predicted survival (90% power, one-sided exact test, alpha .10).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **4-10 untreated brain mets**, age ≥18, **KPS ≥70**, life expectancy >3 mo, DS-GPA ≥0.5, largest lesion ≤4 cm, >2 mm from the optic apparatus. SCLC, germ cell, lymphoma, leukemia, myeloma and leptomeningeal disease were excluded. Median age 61, KPS 90, 6 mets; NSCLC 50%, breast 27.5%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-isocenter VMAT, 1 mm PTV margin, frameless mask, 6DoF couch. PTV <2 cm **20 Gy**, 2 to <3 cm **18 Gy**; PTV >3 cm, brainstem involvement, or brain V12Gy >20 mL moved all lesions to **25 Gy/5 fx**. Median V12Gy 11.7 mL (1 fx), V24Gy 3.5 mL (5 fx); median total hippocampal dose 2.4 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** overall survival. Secondary: local recurrence, distant brain failure, neurologic death, AEs, steroid use; neurocognition and QoL were exploratory.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **mOS 8.1 mo**, 1-yr OS 35.7%; **22 pts** outlived DS-GPA prediction. **1-yr local failure 5%**; distant brain failure 35.8% at 12 mo. Of the 19 pts with distant failure, 15 got salvage (11 SRS, 4 WBRT).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No G3-5** SIMT-related AEs; G1-2 in 73%, headache most common. Radionecrosis in 5 lesions in 4 pts, 2 of whom needed surgery. All 12 pts on steroids before SIMT came off them.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors place median survival in prior multi-met SRS trials at 6.2 to 8.6 mo, so 8.1 mo sits in that range. The randomized SRS vs WBRT question for higher met counts is still open in NCT03550391 (5-15 mets, HA-WBRT), NCT03075072 (5-20) and NCT01592968 (4-15).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with 4-10 mets, good performance status, and lesions up to 4 cm, including brainstem lesions. Does not represent SCLC, leptomeningeal disease, more than 10 mets, or KPS <70.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 11 pts had prior SRS/WBRT, which skews a benchmark that times survival from first brain met diagnosis. Neurocog compliance collapsed after 6 mo (18 deaths before 6 mo), and the paper reports two different 6-mo distant failure figures (20% vs 58%).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: This trial supports the feasibility and safety of a volume-adapted single-isocenter workflow more than any survival claim. Whether SRS alone beats HA-WBRT on neurocognition at 4-10 mets is left to the randomized trials.

studies.interpretation:
The survival endpoint is what this trial is built around, and it is the weakest part. Showing that 22 of 40 pts outlived their DS-GPA estimate, against a prespecified bar of 17, shows that single-isocenter treatment did not obviously harm anyone, measured against a prognostic model built on an older era. The authors say themselves that the original DS-GPA, not the molecular revisions, was used because molecular data were usually missing. In a 2017 to 2019 cohort on modern systemic therapy, many pts would be expected to outlive an older model. The 11 pts with prior brain RT make it worse: their clock started at protocol SRS while the model's starts at first brain met diagnosis. So the noninferiority result says little about whether SRS alone matches WBRT at 4-10 mets. The trial was not designed to answer that question.

The useful content is the dose-adaptation rule. Many centers already treat 4-10 mets with a single isocenter. The open question is when to give up on single fraction. Here the trigger was mechanical: brain V12Gy over 20 mL, any brainstem lesion, or a PTV over 3 cm moved every lesion to 25 Gy/5 fx. Those 79 lesions had 98% local control and 1.3% radionecrosis, against 93% and 3.4% for undiluted single fraction, with the LC difference not significant. The fractionated group also carried larger treatment volumes. Volume-driven fractionation does not appear to cost local control, but the event counts are too small to compare the arms, and the paper says there were too few events to model local failure or necrosis properly.

In practice, the targeting accuracy finding counts for more than it seems. Median longest inter-target distance was 12.0 cm, a setting where rotational error at a single isocenter could erode margins. A 1 mm PTV margin and 1-yr local failure of 5% suggest the 6DoF-corrected linac workflow held up. This only applies to a comparable delivery chain.

Distant brain failure is where readers should be careful. The Results give 6- and 12-mo cumulative incidence of 20% and 35.8% (competing-risk method), but the Discussion cites 58% at 6 mo. The competing-risk figure is the one to use, but the inconsistency should lower confidence in the rest of the reporting. Neurocognitive preservation is reported only for the subset still testing at 3 mo, after a cohort where 18 pts died before 6 mo, so selection toward fitter survivors is likely.

The result would be wrong if the DS-GPA overestimated mortality enough that any reasonable treatment cleared the bar, or if pts who stopped testing were the ones losing cognition. The randomized trials the authors list, including the HA-WBRT comparison at 5-15 mets, are where the SRS-alone decision gets settled. Until then this is a reasonable dosing template, not evidence that SRS alone matches whole-brain treatment.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The volume trigger is the transferable rule: brain V12Gy >20 mL or a brainstem lesion moved all lesions to 25 Gy/5 fx, with 98% vs 93% per-lesion LC and 1.3% vs 3.4% radionecrosis against single fraction. Fractionation depends on aggregate volume, not met count.

studies.name: HyperArc vs manual VMAT SRS: automated planning and delivery
studies.tldr: Paddick GI 5.42 vs 7.09 (P<.001) favoring automated HyperArc over expert manual VMAT SRS; conformity equal; 1-yr LC 90.1% in HyperArc brain mets.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective comparison: 693 single-isocenter VMAT SRS pts, HyperArc vs historical manual VMAT (mVMAT) cohort
🔍 PTV=GTV, no margin, for both techniques; single isocenter for multiple targets
🔍 Brain mets dosing: 18-20 Gy x1, or 30 Gy/5fx if any lesion >2-3 cm or deep

details.text: 📊 Plan quality, QA and workflow, HyperArc vs mVMAT (medians unless stated)
📐 Gradient index advantage holds at matched table-angle count

details: 📊 HyperArc clinical cohort: 107 pts, 377 mets, 1-yr LC 90.1% with 47 tumors at risk
📊 G3 seizures in 3 pts after median clinical f/u 7 mo; no G4/5 events
⚠️ LC cohort is HyperArc-only; no mVMAT clinical comparator, so 'no compromise' in LC is not tested
⚠️ Median imaging f/u 5 mo; 1-yr LC rests on 47 tumors at risk
⚠️ Confound: HyperArc on Eclipse 15.5 vs mVMAT on Eclipse 13.6, sequential eras
⚠️ Multiple authors report Varian grants, fees or patents

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-center historical comparison on dosimetric surrogates; LC from a HyperArc-only cohort with 5-mo median imaging f/u and no manual-VMAT clinical comparator.
verdict.audience: Brain mets (incl. multiple targets) treated with single-isocenter linac SRS

studies.significance: The gradient advantage survives matching arc number: Paddick GI 3.68 vs 4.67 with 2 table angles and 7.53 vs 9.58 with 4, so extra noncoplanar arcs do not explain it. With PTV=GTV single-isocenter delivery and 1-yr LC 90.1%, this supports automated planning for multi-target SRS where planner experience is the bottleneck.
studies.monday_clinic: In pts with multiple brain mets planned for single-isocenter linac SRS with no PTV margin, this supports automated planning matching an expert planner's conformity; it does not address benign or vascular targets, or comparison with Gamma Knife.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution retrospective comparison of **693 pts** with single-isocenter VMAT SRS: 23 pilot + 350 HyperArc pts vs **320 consecutive manual VMAT pts** from the 15 months before adoption. Clinical LC and toxicity were assessed in a **HyperArc-only subgroup of 107 pts / 377 mets**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Of 693 plans, 59.9% had a single target and 12.0% had 6 to 22 targets; target-size distributions did not differ between techniques (P>.99). Most common histologies in the clinical cohort were lung cancer, breast cancer and melanoma.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **PTV=GTV, no margin**, single isocenter, 10 MV FFF on an Edge linac with HD120 MLC, open-mask immobilization. Brain mets got **18-20 Gy x1**, or **30 Gy/5fx** if any lesion exceeded 2-3 cm or involved deep structures; HyperArc used 2 to 4 arcs.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Per-target RTOG and Paddick conformity, Paddick gradient, falloff index, bridging, mean normal-brain dose, modulation factor, film-based PSQA, and timestamp-derived planning, imaging and delivery times. LC defined as no 25% diameter increase on MRI, scored per lesion; toxicity per CTCAE v5.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Conformity was equivalent and the **gradient index was lower with HyperArc**; arm-level values are in the detail table. Isodose bridging at the 50% level occurred in 10.8% vs 13.1% of targets.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **G3 seizures in 3 pts**, no G4/5 events, after median clinical f/u of 7 mo; toxicity was scored retrospectively from chart review.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Manual plans followed the published Clark et al single-isocenter class solution with the Thomas et al low-dose-spill penalty, which this group had previously reported as comparable to clinical Gamma Knife plans. **No Gamma Knife arm here**, so the benchmark is an expert in-house manual linac technique, not GK.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents brain mets, including multi-target cases, treated with single-isocenter linac SRS and no PTV margin at an experienced center. Does not represent benign or vascular targets (no clinical data reported) or comparison with Gamma Knife or multi-isocenter approaches.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Techniques ran on different Eclipse versions (15.5 vs 13.6) in consecutive eras, so software and learning effects confound the gradient difference. Planning time was a timestamp surrogate in a clinic with 9 years of manual experience, and several authors have Varian financial ties.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for automation here is **standardization**: equal conformity, a modestly steeper gradient, and slightly shorter room time. The clinical value of a lower gradient index, and the rotational-error risk for targets far from isocenter with no margin, remain open.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a standardization argument rather than a superiority claim. The manual comparator is not a weak straw man: it is an in-house single-isocenter class solution built on the Clark et al nested-tuning-structure approach and refined with an explicit low-dose brain spill penalty, run by a clinic with 9 years of experience. Matching that on conformity (RTOG 1.14 vs 1.13) while posting a lower Paddick gradient index (5.42 vs 7.09) says the automated optimizer reaches expert-level plans without the months of planner training that manual multi-target SRS usually needs. That is the transferable finding, and it matters more at centers without such a planner than at this one.

The gradient result deserves the most scrutiny because it is the only plan-quality metric that clearly moved. The obvious objection is that HyperArc plans used more arcs (median 3 vs 2), and more noncoplanar entry naturally steepens falloff. The authors address this directly: stratifying by table-angle count, the difference persists at 2 angles (3.68 vs 4.67) and at 4 angles (7.53 vs 9.58). That stratification is the strongest piece of evidence in the paper. What it cannot remove is the era confound: HyperArc plans ran on Eclipse 15.5 and manual plans on 13.6, so some of the gradient gain may belong to the platform rather than the automated objective. The mean brain dose difference (4.6% vs 5.1%) is small, and the distributions did not differ, so a reader should not convert the gradient gain into a claim about radionecrosis or neurocognition. No such endpoint was measured.

The clinical data are the weakest part and should be weighted accordingly. Local control of 90.1% at 1 year comes only from HyperArc-treated mets, with a median imaging follow-up of 5 months and 47 tumors at risk at the 1-year mark. There is no manual-VMAT clinical arm, so the conclusion that a no-margin single-isocenter approach did not compromise outcomes is a statement of consistency with historical expectation, not a comparison. Three grade 3 seizures with no grade 4 or 5 events is reassuring for an early cohort but is retrospectively scored from charts.

The question the paper flags but cannot answer is geometric. Treating many targets anywhere in the brain from one isocenter with zero margin relies on tight rotational alignment, and small rotations translate into larger displacements for distant lesions. This group manages that with 6-degree-of-freedom couch correction and short delivery times; other centers add margin or split isocenters. Before generalizing, a reader would want lesion-level local control stratified by distance from isocenter, longer follow-up, and toxicity outcomes tied to the gradient metrics. The workflow gains (room time 10.5 vs 11.4 minutes) are real but modest, and planning time did not differ in expert hands, which leaves the less-experienced-planner benefit as a reasonable inference rather than something this study demonstrated.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The gradient advantage persists at matched table-angle count (Paddick GI 3.68 vs 4.67 at 2 angles), so it is not just extra arcs. With PTV=GTV single-isocenter delivery and 1-yr LC 90.1%, this supports automated planning for multi-target SRS where planner experience limits plan quality.

open_questions: Does the lower gradient index translate into less radionecrosis?

papers.title: Transition From Manual to Automated Planning and Delivery of Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Clinical, Dosimetric, and Quality Assurance Results
Interinstitutional Plan Quality Assessment of 2 Linac-Based, Single-Isocenter, Multiple Metastasis Radiosurgery Techniques
Outcomes in Patients With 4 to 10 Brain Metastases Treated With Dose-Adapted Single-Isocenter Multitarget Stereotactic Radiosurgery: A Prospective Study
Initial Experience With Single-Isocenter Radiosurgery to Target Multiple Brain Metastases Using an Automated Treatment Planning Software: Clinical Outcomes and Optimal Target Volume Margins Strategy
Dosimetric comparison among dynamic conformal arc therapy, coplanar and non-coplanar volumetric modulated arc therapy for single brain metastasis
papers.abstract: Abstract In the delivery of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) by linear accelerator (LINAC), dynamic conformal arc therapy (DCAT) with non-coplanar beams is conventionally used. However, volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) can improve target conformity, thereby decreasing the dose to organs at risk by inversed planning methods, but few studies have directly compared DCAT and VMAT with and without non-coplanar beams in patients with single brain metastasis. We therefore conducted a planning study to compare the dose distribution in DCAT, VMAT using only a coplanar arc (CoVMAT) and VMAT with non-coplanar arcs (NcVMAT) in the treatment of single brain metastasis. DCAT, CoVMAT and NcVMAT plans were created for 15 patients. The three modalities were compared in terms of target conformity, target coverage, the dose to normal brain tissue, monitor units (MUs) and beam-on time. Both conformity indices (RTOG-CI and IP-CI) as well as the D98% of the gross target volume (GTV) were significantly better in the NcVMAT plans than in the DCAT plans. Comparisons of the doses to normal brain tissue revealed that the V20Gy, V15Gy, V12Gy, V10Gy and V5Gy were significantly smaller in the NcVMAT plans than in the plans based on the other two modalities. The MUs of the DCAT and NcVMAT plans were larger than those of the CoVMAT plans, and the beam-on time was longer in the NcVMAT and CoVMAT plans than in the DCAT plans. Compared to the CoVMAT and DCAT plans, NcVMAT plans significantly improved target conformity and reduced the doses to normal brain tissue at V20Gy, V15Gy, V12Gy, V10Gy and V5Gy.
